blockingProblems: SELF-CONTRADICTION ON THE ORGANIZING ORDINAL. Paragraph 2 promises: 'The fourth has every input the recipe asks for, is carried out exactly as written, and fails at a step.' The chapter then opens the quantum-criticality section with 'The second case is the one where nothing is missing' and 'The failure, when it comes, is at the step and not at the inputs,' and opens the spin-glass section with 'The fourth case is the one that will matter most later in this book.' The closing paragraph reconfirms the presentation ordering ('The fourth breaks a symmetry among $n$ copies'). So 'the fourth' names the quantum critical point in the framing paragraph and the spin glass everywhere else. The chapter's own thesis statement points the reader at the wrong section, and it does so in the paragraph whose entire job is to install the taxonomy.

SECOND CONTRADICTION IN THE SAME TAXONOMY. Paragraph 2 asserts 'Three of the four transitions collected here are missing an input.' The percolation section opens 'The third case strips away not one ingredient but the entire apparatus,' and then enumerates that percolation has no Hamiltonian, no temperature, no free energy and no symmetry. Losing the whole apparatus is not an instance of 'missing an input'; the chapter is aware of this (it says so explicitly) and never reconciles it with the frame it just built.

THE TAXONOMY DOES NOT SURVIVE ITS OWN TEST CASE. The framing claims the three input-failures are each 'missing a different one.' BKT and the spin glass are missing the same input: a local order parameter that is an average over sites. What differs is the replacement (a loop integral of the winding number versus a self-overlap in time), not the missing input. The chapter has the material to make this distinction sharply and instead states a stronger, false version of it. Separately, the spin glass also fails at a step: the replica-symmetric saddle point is the natural choice and it is wrong, which is what the negative entropy reports. The chapter's own two-failure-modes scheme therefore does not partition its four cases, and the chapter never notices.

CONVENTIONAL EPONYM USED WITHOUT NAMING IT. The passage 'it fixes $\rho(T_c^-) = 2k_BT_c/\pi$, a value that depends on nothing but the transition temperature... the stiffness falls discontinuously, by an amount that is universal' is the Nelson-Kosterlitz universal jump, and the result is not named. This is the chapter's single best physics paragraph and the one place it withholds the standard label. The packet has no Nelson and Kosterlitz 1977 entry, so the fix is a packet addition, not a deletion of the physics.

LENGTH. Body word count, counting each inline and display math expression as a single word and including section headings, is 3,903, above the 3,800 ceiling. Reproducibility note for the author: a raw file word count on the body is 4,025 (LaTeX tokens counted individually); stripping math and headings gives a floor of 3,757. Every reasonable convention except the most permissive one puts the chapter over.
styleViolations: Clean on the hard prohibitions: zero em dashes, zero double hyphens, zero bullet or numbered lists in the body. Verified mechanically.

One disguised list rendered as a 60-word sentence: 'The Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition is therefore invisible to the diagnostics Landau's framework supplies, since there is no symmetry breaking, no local order parameter, and no power-law divergence of the correlation length, and it is perfectly visible to a quantity the framework never asks for.' Two coordinated clauses each carrying an internal three-item inventory. It is the least readable sentence in the chapter and it sits on the chapter's most important claim.

Repeated construction: 'The correction took four years to arrive' (Mermin-Wagner to Berezinskii) and 'The negative entropy is a signal, and reading it took four years' (Sherrington-Kirkpatrick to Parisi). Both are true and both are good beats; using the identical figure and cadence twice makes the second read as a tic rather than a rhyme.

The penultimate passage ('Two of them have no broken symmetry at all. A third... The fourth...') re-inventories all four cases in sequence. It is doing argumentative work against Anderson's thesis rather than merely summarizing, so I do not score it as a recap, but it sits one revision away from being one.

Closing line: 'Ensembles are the one thing this subject is no longer short of.' The referent is unstable. If it means statistical ensembles it is a shrug; if it is a wink at machine-learning ensembles it is a pun on two unrelated technical senses of the word, in a chapter that is otherwise scrupulous about not conflating shared vocabulary. Either way it lands soft after a strong paragraph.
factProblems: No false statements found. I checked every attribution, date, venue, author order and numerical result against the packet, and every derivation for internal consistency. Citation hygiene is above monograph standard: all five packet CORRECTED/REFUTED items that bear on this chapter are applied. The Berezinskii Russian original is dated 1970 with the 1971 translation; the 2021 Nobel citation reads 'complex physical systems'; the Sauer translation is EPJ Special Topics 226, 539-549 (2017); the Guerra sign convention is stated in the exact form the REFUTED entry prescribes, including the explanatory gloss; the two 1987 Huse-Fisher / Fisher-Huse author-order flips are correct; and no affiliation is printed for Millis, whose affiliation the packet marks UNVERIFIABLE. No affiliations are printed anywhere, which sidesteps the packet's Rushbrooke, Lee-Yang, Lieb-Sokal and Clapeyron traps.

Arithmetic and derivations verified: the spin-wave prefactor $k_BT/\rho$, the $d=1,2,3$ behaviour of the mode sum, $E_1 = \pi\rho\ln(L/a)$, $S_1 = 2k_B\ln(L/a)$, the sign change at $k_BT_c = \pi\rho/2$, the consistency of $\eta = k_BT/(2\pi\rho)$ with $\eta = 1/4$ at $T_c$, $d+z = 6$ and $5$ against an upper critical dimension of four, $q(x)$ as the inverse cumulative distribution of $P(q)$, $P(q)$ as delta functions at $\pm m^2$ in a ferromagnet, and the ultrametric inequality restated as the isosceles-triangle condition. All correct.

Two unattributed characterizations of the literature. 'Lars Onsager's exact two-dimensional solution... is usually presented as a correction to the mean-field exponents rather than as a refutation of the framework' and 'That last case is the one usually described least accurately.' Both are claims about how other authors have handled this material, and neither names a text. The second is the load-bearing justification for the chapter's most ambitious section. This is the soft form of criticizing published work without naming papers, and it should either name a textbook treatment or be recast as a claim about what the physics implies rather than about what other people say.

Minor imprecision: 'a three-dimensional metal sits at or above the upper critical dimension.' At $d=3$, both $z=3$ and $z=2$ give $d+z > 4$ strictly; 'at' has no referent in the case under discussion.

Minor chronological softness: 'Talagrand supplied the matching bound, announcing the result in 2003 and publishing the full proof in 2006, at which point Parisi's formula for the free energy became a theorem.' The packet notes the 2003 Comptes Rendus announcement carries the full statement, and flags the 2002-2003 Guerra-to-Talagrand gap as the striking interval. 'At which point' quietly awards the theorem to 1906-style publication rather than to the announcement, without saying so.

Structural gap rather than a factual error: the chapter belongs to a book about AI and phase transitions and does not mention machine learning, learned representations, or the book's demo once. Its only connective tissue is 'The fourth case is the one that will matter most later in this book,' with no indication of how or where. The packet's stated payload for this chapter ('where human intuition about order parameters runs out'; 'directly ancestral to Part Six'; 'What else are we failing to guess?') is never cashed. As written this is an excellent freestanding condensed-matter essay that would sit unchanged in someone else's monograph.
whatWouldMakeItAAA: The physics writing here is genuinely at press standard and the citation discipline is above it, so the gap to AAA is narrow and almost entirely architectural. First, repair the frame. Rewrite paragraph 2 so the taxonomy is true of the four cases it introduces and stops colliding with the section ordinals: name the case that fails at a step by what it is ('the quantum critical point of an itinerant magnet') rather than by an ordinal, drop 'each is missing a different one' in favour of the distinction the chapter can actually defend (BKT and the spin glass both lack a site-averaged order parameter, but the quantity that replaces it is a loop integral in one case and a self-overlap in time in the other), and stop calling percolation a missing input when the chapter itself says three sections later that it strips away the whole apparatus. Then concede, in one sentence, that the spin glass fails at both an input and a step, because a taxonomy that admits its one overlapping case is more convincing than one that pretends the partition is clean. Second, name the Nelson-Kosterlitz jump and add the 1977 paper to the packet; the derivation is the strongest passage in the chapter and it is the one result presented anonymously. Third, replace the two unattributed 'usually' claims with either a named treatment or a claim about the physics; 'that last case is the one usually described least accurately' is the chapter's warrant for its most ambitious section and it currently rests on nobody. Fourth, cut roughly 150 words, and take them from the disguised-list sentence about BKT's invisibility, which should become two sentences, and from the percolation section, which recites exponents at more length than a control experiment needs. Fifth, cash the forward reference: one sentence saying what about the spin glass returns later, and in what form, would convert a bare promise into a real hook and would begin to make this chapter belong to this book rather than to the genre. Finally, replace the last line. The Anderson frame-close is a real move and the ensemble observation that precedes it is the chapter's best synthetic claim; end on that claim sharpened, not on a pun whose referent the reader cannot pin down.
